title: Knight forks in combination
objectives: Recognize when a fork isn't available yet but a preparatory forcing move can set one up
Play a forcing move that drives a king toward a square your knight can fork
Find a knight fork that only becomes available after an earlier capture in the position
Distinguish a real fork that wins material from a square that forks two pieces where one is defended

steps.text: Not every fork is sitting on the board waiting for you — sometimes you have to create one. In this position, no single knight move forks the king and the rook yet. But a forcing move first (a check that the king has to answer) can drive the king onto a square your knight can then fork. Preparing a fork is just as much a real skill as spotting one.

steps.prompt: If a knight fork isn't available on the board right now, there's nothing you can do to create one.

feedback.default: A forcing move — a check, a capture, a threat the opponent must answer — can drive a piece (often the king) onto a square your knight then forks. Forks aren't only found; they're often built.

steps.successExplanation: Right — a well-timed forcing move can drive the king or another piece onto exactly the square your knight needs.

steps.prompt: Play the bishop move that gives check, then — after Black's king moves — find the knight move that forks the king and the rook.
steps.successExplanation: Bd5+ forces the king toward a7 — the only reasonable answer to the check. From there, Nb5+ forks the king on a7 and the rook on d6 at the same time, winning the exchange. Neither move alone was a fork; together, they created one.

steps.prompt: This position followed a trade a move ago — Black's queen just recaptured on b5. Find the knight move that forks the king and the queen.

hints.text: The queen just landed on b5 to recapture — it hasn't had time to notice a knight fork is now available.
One square attacks both the king and the queen at once.
Nc7+ forks the king on e8 and the queen on b5 — a fork that only existed because the queen had just recaptured onto a forkable square.

feedback.default: That doesn't fork both pieces. Find the single square your knight can jump to that attacks the king and the queen at the same time.

steps.successExplanation: Nc7+ forks the king and the queen. This fork didn't exist before the recapture on b5 — recognizing a fork that appears mid-combination, not just on a fresh position, is exactly the skill this lesson is building.

steps.prompt: Two knight moves both give check and both attack a rook — but only one of them actually wins material. Find it.

hints.text: Both Ne7+ and Nf6+ fork the king and a rook — but check whether each rook is actually undefended before deciding.
One of these two rooks has a defender; the other doesn't.
Play the fork that wins material for real.
Ne7+ forks the king and the undefended rook on c8. Nf6+ also forks the king and a rook, but the rook on e8 is defended by the bishop on d7 — that fork only trades pieces evenly.

feedback.default: That's a legal knight move, but check carefully whether the rook it forks is actually undefended — a fork that only wins a defended piece isn't a real win.

steps.successExplanation: Ne7+ forks the king on g8 and the undefended rook on c8 — real material won. Nf6+ looks identical at first glance, but the rook it forks on e8 is defended by the bishop on d7, so that version only trades evenly. A fork isn't automatically winning; check what the forked piece is actually worth losing.

steps.prompt: You find a knight move that forks the enemy king and a rook. What should you check before assuming you've won material?
options: Nothing — any fork on the king always wins material
Whether the rook (or whatever else is forked) is actually undefended, since a fork on a defended piece only trades
Whether the knight itself is defended

feedback.default: A fork guarantees the opponent can't save both pieces at once — but if the non-king target is defended, 'losing' it just means an even trade, not free material.

steps.successExplanation: Right — always check whether the forked piece is actually undefended. Forking two pieces isn't automatically winning if one of them can simply be recaptured.

steps.summary: A knight fork doesn't have to already be sitting on the board — a forcing move can drive a piece onto a square you can then fork, and a fork can appear mid-combination, right after an earlier capture changed the position. Once you find a forking square, always double-check that what you're forking is actually undefended — a fork on a defended piece only trades material, it doesn't win it.
